content: Tipedine, also known by its International Nonproprietary Name (INN), is a synthetic, non-opioid antitussive (cough suppressant) and expectorant belonging to the thiambutene class. It is marketed under various brand names, including Asverin, Antupex, Asvelik, Asvex, Bitiodin, Cofdenin A, Hustel, Nodal, and Sotal. Additionally, it is referred to as tipedine hibenzoate in Japan (JAN). This drug functions as an inhibitor of G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs). Tipedine was first discovered in the 1950s and subsequently developed in Japan in 1959. It is typically administered in the form of hibenzoate or citrate salts. The standard dosage is 20 mg every 4 to 6 hours. Potential side effects of tipedine, particularly in cases of overdose, include drowsiness, vertigo, delirium, disorientation, loss of consciousness, and confusion. Recently, tipedine has attracted attention as a potential psychiatric medication. It is currently being studied for its possible applications in treating depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). By inhibiting GIRK channels, tipedine increases dopamine levels in the nucleus accumbens. However, this increase in dopamine does not lead to heightened locomotor activity or methamphetamine-like behavioral sensitization. This mechanism is thought to contribute, at least in part, to its antidepressant-like effects observed in rodent studies.
